message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Category | What You’re Generally Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |----------|-----------------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord keeps any portion. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc.). | • Report problems in writing (email or letter).
• If the landlord fails to fix, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable (usually not more than 5% of the rent). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter your unit without **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any unannounced entries. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must respect your privacy; they can’t monitor your activities or tamper with personal belongings. | • Report any violations to the landlord or local authorities. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice of non‑renewal at least **30 days** before the lease ends. | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable time, etc.). | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a **30‑day notice** for non‑payment of rent or a **60‑day notice** for lease violations.
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an eviction lawsuit. | • Respond to notices promptly; consider mediation or legal counsel. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide a written statement of who pays which utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • You may sublet or assign the lease only with the landlord’s written consent (unless the lease prohibits it). | • Obtain written permission before moving out or subletting. | | **Landlord’s Right to Inspect** | • Landlord may inspect the unit with **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) for maintenance or to show to prospective tenants. | • Keep a record of inspection dates and purposes. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If the landlord violates your rights, you can file a complaint with TDHCA, TCHR, or HUD, or pursue a civil action in court. | • Keep all documentation (photos, emails, receipts). | ### Quick Tips for Protecting Your Rights 1. **Read the Lease Carefully** – Make sure it complies with Texas statutes (e.g., security deposit limits, notice periods). 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written communication, and receipts help if disputes arise. 3. **Know the Timeline** – Texas law sets specific notice periods for rent increases, repairs, and evictions. 4. **Use Written Communication** – Email or certified mail provides a paper trail. 5. **Seek Help Early** – If you’re facing a potential eviction or serious habitability issue, contact a local tenant‑rights group or legal aid clinic. ### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | Contact | |----------|----------------|---------| | Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) | Tenant‑landlord dispute resolution, housing code enforcement | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us/ | | Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) | Discrimination complaints | https://www.tchr.texas.gov/ | | U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) | Fair Housing complaints | https://www.hud.gov/ | | Texas Legal Services Center | Free legal advice for low‑income residents | https://www.texaslegalservices.org/ | | Local tenant‑rights organizations (e.g., Texas Tenants Union) | Advocacy, workshops, legal clinics | Search online for your city | --- **Disclaimer:** This information is intended for general informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Laws can change, and specific circumstances may alter how the law applies. If you have a particular issue or need personalized guidance, consider consulting a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
